values:
Scope note

Rows identify named or otherwise source-resolvable projects. They are not anonymous permit placeholders. Permit/building-flow totals are stored on the Annual Estimates sheet and should be used as historical denominators, not expanded into fictional building entities.
Rare North Side post-fire architecture; sources report work began before a February 1872 code update, but permit evidence remains to be acquired.
Preservation Chicago documents the 1872 date and demolition; exact demolition month and original owner require archival verification.
Adams Street bridge rendered impassable in 1871 fire
Municipal infrastructure funded partly through Illinois canal-refund appropriation.
One of eight named bridges repaired immediately and completed within one year of the fire.
Entertainment replacement after the fire; address and construction material unresolved.
Opened October 7 1872 with a series of concerts; Andreas supports opening but fuller building description requires theater-history follow-up.
northeast corner Randolph Street and Michigan Avenue; 102 Michigan Avenue
Post-fire masonry commercial reconstruction; exact code compliance unverified.
A June 1872 notice describes a five-story 90-by-130-foot building; Chicago Burlington & Quincy occupied the upper four stories in December. Chicagology rebuilding008.
South Park Avenue near Twenty-third Street
Industrial expansion outside principal burned core.
Large addition to brewery proper made in 1871-72; phase endpoint is recorded as 1872 but exact month unknown.
Bemis and McAvoy Brewery Ice House No. 1
west side South Park Avenue near Twenty-third Street
Industrial addition outside principal burned core; no direct code claim.
One of a sequence of west-side ice houses explicitly dated 1872, 1874, 1875 and 1876; only the 1872 unit is recorded here.
Twenty-fourth Street between Michigan and Indiana Avenues
downtown Bournique academy destroyed in 1871 fire
Brick replacement outside the core burned district.
Erected in summer 1872; capacity doubled in 1874. Not to be confused with the 1882-84 Twenty-third Street academy.
Industrial construction west of the core burned district; no direct fire-code evidence.
Andreas states Brachvogel built the factory structure occupied by the later company in 1872; street-number continuity should be checked against directories.
north side Madison Street between Clark and LaSalle Streets
Contemporary description emphasized fire plugs and two fireproof vaults but complete fire resistance is not inferred.
Opened in November 1872 with 125 sleeping rooms; later hotel identity and a south adjoining A. Crocker building must remain separate. Chicagology rebuilding113.
southwest corner State and Madison Streets
Buck and Rayner Building fire-damaged in 1871
Reconstruction incorporated surviving pre-fire walls; not wholly new construction.
Rebuilt immediately after the fire and photographed in August 1872; later source says part of the 1868 walls survived. Chicagology rebuilding116.
C. L. Rice and Company Machine Shops and Warerooms
Dearborn/Madison machinery premises destroyed in 1871 fire
Industrial relocation west of the core burned district.
Construction began at once after the fire; occupied in fall 1872 and business sold to Kirkwood and Dunklee about then.
C. M. Henderson and Company Building
southeast corner Franklin and Madison Streets; formerly 235 Madison
Masonry warehouse in the new post-fire wholesale district.
Contemporary September 1872 feature documents the new building; exact completion date and demolition year remain approximate. Chicagology rebuilding097.
Central European Hotel destroyed in 1871 fire; temporary frame shanty
Brick replacement following an immediate temporary frame shanty; fire-limit status requires historic parcel review.
Andreas OCR says the temporary shanty was replaced 'next year' by the present brick structure; interpreted as 1872 but flagged for scan verification.
southeast corner Washington and LaSalle Streets
Chamber of Commerce I destroyed in 1871 fire
Prominent masonry reconstruction inside the fire limits.
Completed before and formally occupied on the fire's first anniversary, October 9 1872; Andreas reports cost about $365,000.
Chicago Avenue bridge rendered impassable in 1871 fire
Municipal infrastructure funded partly through Illinois canal-refund appropriation.
One of eight named bridges repaired immediately and completed within one year of the fire.
Chicago Society of the New Jerusalem West Division Church
Chicago Society of the New Jerusalem
Outside the core burned business district; no direct fire-code claim.
Andreas calls it a commodious house of worship built in 1872; the society later sold the Ogden frontage in 1885.
southeast corner Dearborn and Madison Streets
masonry; iron roof; largely noncombustible floors
Tribune Building I destroyed in 1871 fire
Explicitly designed as a more genuinely fire-resistant replacement, with iron roof and tile, asphalt or artificial-marble floors.
Occupied October 8-9 1872 while final work continued about another month; 72 by 121 feet. Chicagology page rebuilding030 transcribes the contemporary Tribune account.
139-141 Monroe Street between Clark and LaSalle Streets
brick with stone basement; white Wisconsin-brick front
Chicago Type Foundry destroyed in 1871 fire
Substantial masonry factory reconstruction in the fire district.
Construction began about March 1 and moving began May 6 1872; 45 by 80 feet. Chicagology rebuilding057/rebuilding108 transcribes the company account.
masonry shell repaired; iron roof substituted
Iron roof replaced the combustible covering; Andreas reports total repair-related cost about $248,410 including system losses.
Machine shop reconstructed, engines returned to service, hydrants/meters repaired and iron roof installed during first post-fire year; treated as a complex phase.
Clark Street bridge rendered impassable in 1871 fire
Municipal infrastructure funded partly through Illinois canal-refund appropriation.
One of eight named bridges repaired immediately and completed within one year of the fire.
Clark Street viaduct rendered impassable in 1871 fire
Municipal infrastructure funded partly through Illinois canal-refund appropriation.
One of three named viaducts repaired immediately and completed within one year of the fire.
northwest corner Dearborn and Lake Streets
Couch estate; William H. Ward trustee; High & Magie adjoining interests
stone front; five-story corner and four-story additions
Permanent masonry construction within the burned district.
Built for American Express, which declined occupancy; Howell Pulling and Hiram F. Ingraham opened the combined structure as Commercial Hotel in 1872; about 270 rooms by 1886.
Convent of Saints Benedict and Scholastica Home
corner North Market and Hill Streets
St. Joseph parish church and school destroyed in 1871 fire
Frame institutional rebuilding undertaken immediately after the fire; location and permission context need ordinance research.
Finished in 1872 and later enlarged with a brick rear addition in 1879; institution incorporated July 1 1872.
Convent of the Immaculate Conception II
convent and school destroyed in 1871 fire
Institutional replacement in the North Side fire area; material not established.
Dominican Sisters returned in 1872 and erected the building after Bishop Foley promised assistance; later adjoining parochial school excluded.
Cregier Pumping Engine at Chicago Water Works
DeWitt Cregier; Knapp Fort Pitt Foundry Works
Post-fire capacity and resilience upgrade; building-code context not applicable.
Completed and started November 27 1872 through a 36-inch main; engine and boilers cost $188,400.
Fidelity Savings Bank and Safe Depository II
Banking reconstruction in the fire district; specific fireproof systems need verification.
Chicagology rebuilding109 identifies the 1872 building and contemporary banking occupancy; precise completion evidence should be checked in the original newspaper.
worship, stores, offices and meeting hall
First Methodist block destroyed in 1871 fire
More substantial post-fire replacement in the burned district; rental uses funded church operations.
Congregation left its temporary Clark-and-Harrison frame building in fall 1872 for the rebuilt block; cost about $130,000. Chicagology rebuilding072 and Chicago History Museum corroborate context.
southwest corner State and Washington Streets
iron, stone and brick; surviving vaults
First National Bank Building II fire-damaged in 1871
Reused surviving walls and vaults; contemporary descriptions called it fireproof but Andreas cautions that such claims were unsettled.
Restored in 1872 for about $75,000 of a reported $295,000 total building value; the pre-fire fifth floor was not restored. Chicagology rebuilding177 transcribes contemporary sources.
Andreas calls it essentially fireproof in its later form, but later alterations and fire escapes should not be retrojected to 1872.
Finished and opened October 1 1872, the first American-plan hotel opened in the burned district; cost including ground reported about $600,000.
southeast corner Lake and Market Streets
rental property supporting Garrett Biblical Institute
Masonry rebuilding in the fire district.
Contemporary notices describe a roughly 130-by-180-foot four-story building, cost about $100,000, with portions ready for tenants in August. Chicagology rebuilding175.
Industrial addition outside principal burned core.
Built in 1872; a second ice house belongs to 1879 and later brewery reconstruction to 1884-85.
southwest corner Wabash Avenue and Lake Street
Permanent mercantile rebuilding in the fire district.
Chicagology rebuilding112 gives a 1872 life span start and contemporary directory evidence; exact completion date needs original source review.
Hall's Safe and Lock Company Building
147-149 Dearborn Street between Madison and Monroe Streets
Hall company building destroyed in 1871 fire
Rebuilt on the old site in masonry; the safe-company use made post-fire fire resistance central to its marketing.
Contemporary June 1872 account says the firm was back on its old site eight months after the fire. Chicagology rebuilding114.
Post-fire Near West Side construction; the source links the building to rapid development after the fire without claiming it stood in the burned district.
Rare surviving Italianate commercial block with date and Holden name carved at the roofline.
Wabash Avenue between Harrison and Congress Streets
Located south of the principal burned district; direct code context not established.
Chicagology rebuilding110 identifies the 1872-1874 building; destroyed in the 1874 fire. Original contemporary notice requires image-level verification.
J. V. Farwell & Company Block III
northwest corner Monroe and Franklin Streets; extension toward Market Street
brick masonry; experimental cement wall sections
Farwell commercial property lost in 1871 fire
Built immediately after the fire; Andreas documents an experimental poured-cement wall method using rubble fill.
First section completed about three months after the fire; a 1872 extension formed a 191-by-235-foot complex. Chicagology rebuilding071 distinguishes the phases.
George E. Woodward pattern-book Design No. 2
wood-frame Second Empire house; mansard roof
Outside Chicago's 1872 municipal limits and outside the burned district; no post-fire ordinance inference.

Official City source dates the house circa 1872. Included because it lies within present Chicago and documents Irving Park's railroad-suburb development; historical-jurisdiction flag should be retained.
246-252 Madison Street near Market Street; later 323-331 West Madison
wholesale hats, caps, furs and millinery
Keith Brothers premises destroyed in 1871 fire
Stone wholesale reconstruction in the expanded post-fire business district.
Contemporary August and October 1872 accounts describe the nearly finished 55-by-170-foot building; occupancy followed within weeks. Chicagology rebuilding180.
Dearborn Street in the burned district
Thomas Mackin and Samuel Gregsten leasehold; William J. Kuhns operator
First European-plan hotel erected in the burned district after the fire.
North 70-foot section built and opened about August 1872; later additions and Windsor identity must be separated from the 1872 phase.
northwest corner LaSalle and Madison Streets
Stone commercial reconstruction in the fire district.
Up to the fourth story October 13 and expected to be occupied in November 1872; final finish extended into 1873. Chicagology rebuilding117.
northwest corner Wabash Avenue and Lake Street
Contemporary February 1872 notice announced Nos. 34-40 Lake; October coverage illustrates it among McCormick structures. Chicagology rebuilding168.
southeast corner Madison and Market Streets; 256-262 Madison
boot and shoe factory and salesrooms
Philadelphia pressed brick with Ohio-stone trim
Permanent masonry rebuilding in the wholesale district.
Completed by August 1872; cost about $100,000 with steam heat, elevators and power. Chicagology rebuilding131.
southeast corner Madison and LaSalle Streets
Major Block I destroyed in 1871 fire
Designed as substantial stone reconstruction with office vaults; direct ordinance inspection not located.
Foundations underway April; intended occupancy October; contemporary October account identifies the completed streetscape. About 66 by 135 feet. Chicagology rebuilding036.
northeast corner Lake and LaSalle Streets
Marine Bank and Mechanics' National Bank
Marine Bank property destroyed in 1871 fire
Permanent bank rebuilding in the fire district.
Ready for roof October 5 1872; occupancy/completion may have followed late that year or early 1873. About 70 by 80 feet; projected cost $95,000. Chicagology rebuilding139.
Post-fire hotel replacement; direct code evidence not located.
Andreas says built by Albert Longley in 1872 and completed and opened in the fall; address is unreadable or absent in the OCR and needs directory follow-up.
northeast corner Wabash Avenue and Jackson Street
pre-fire Matteson House at Randolph and Dearborn Streets
Substantial hotel relocation/replacement after the fire; not on the original site.
Finished late in 1872 but opened February 3 1873; completion and opening are intentionally separated.
Madison Street between State and Dearborn Streets
McVicker's Theatre II destroyed in 1871 fire
Prominent entertainment reconstruction in the burned district.
Under active reconstruction in August and intended for the fall 1872 season; exact opening date should be verified. Chicagology rebuilding045.
Church construction underway before/through the fire era outside the principal burned core.
A portion was formally dedicated February 5 1872; full completion occurred during J. W. Phelps's 1873-74 pastorate, so this is not a full completion.
southeast corner Clark and Madison Streets
Permanent stone commercial replacement in the burned district.
October 1872 description gives 90 by 100 feet and cost over $100,000; a January 1873 illustration shows completed rebuilt streetscape. Chicagology rebuilding103.
northeast corner Clark and Madison Streets
Morrison commercial buildings destroyed in 1871 fire
Permanent stone-front reconstruction within the fire district.
Plans reported February 1872; later account describes the completed building and about $100,000 cost. Distinct from the Morrison Block on the southeast corner. Chicagology rebuilding217.
Oriental Building I destroyed in 1871 fire
Prominent commercial reconstruction in the burned district.
Contemporary May and October 1872 notices document construction and partial occupancy; final completion date needs directory/permit verification. Chicagology rebuilding042.
177-191 North State Street; north facade on Lake Street
Built during the first-year rebuilding under the post-fire fire-limits regime; its surviving cast-iron facade preserves a construction technique common before the fire.
Official City narrative dates the building to 1872; the State Street facade and fifth story are a separate 1902 phase.
166-172 State Street; southwest corner State and Monroe Streets
Stone-and-masonry commercial rebuilding opposite the Palmer House.
Featured as a newly erected block in the October 1872 Land Owner; Chicagology rebuilding104.
Polk Street bridge rendered impassable in 1871 fire
Municipal infrastructure funded partly through Illinois canal-refund appropriation.
One of eight named bridges repaired immediately and completed within one year of the fire.
northeast corner Lake Street and Wabash Avenue
pressed brick; plate glass; galvanized-iron cornice
Hibbard & Spencer premises destroyed in 1871 fire
Permanent mercantile rebuilding in the fire district.
Contemporary April and October 1872 notices document construction and occupancy; footprint about 48 by 140 feet for the occupied portion. Chicagology rebuilding067.
North Park Avenue and Centre Street; later Clark near Centre
Purpose-built from fire relics; not evidence of ordinary code-compliant construction.
Constructed in 1872 from melted iron, glass, pottery and stone and later moved roughly 100 yards. Chicagology rebuilding046.
11-13 Fifth Avenue and 205-207 South Water Street
Permanent commercial rebuilding in the burned district.

Contemporary November 1872 account calls the 80-by-150-foot building rebuilt for about $100,000. Chicagology rebuilding101 also describes a related Lake Street block and a separate Ohio/Franklin manufacturing complex, not merged here.
Rush Street bridge rendered impassable in 1871 fire
Municipal infrastructure funded partly through Illinois canal-refund appropriation.
One of eight named bridges repaired immediately and completed within one year of the fire.
Dutton & Sawyer stables/business disrupted by 1871 fire
Stable construction presented elevated fire risk; material and ordinance compliance are not given.
Built January 1872 and occupied by Sawyer's livery business.
northeast corner Madison and LaSalle Streets; 135 LaSalle
Commercial rebuilding inside the fire district.
Shown as a new 1872 streetscape building; formal Anchor Line office opening occurred January 1873, so construction completion remains approximate. Chicagology rebuilding089.
pre-fire St. Charles Hotel destroyed in 1871 fire
Permanent hotel rebuilding in the fire district.
Andreas explicitly says rebuilt in 1872 and opened by Phil Conley; later Raggio return and remodeling belong to 1878.
St. Matthew's German Evangelical Lutheran Church
block between Twentieth, Twenty-first, Hoyne and Leavitt Streets
St. Matthew's German Evangelical Lutheran Church
brick basement with frame upper story
Mixed brick/frame construction outside the principal fire limits; no ordinance-compliance inference.
Trustees erected the two-story church-school in 1872; later 1875 and 1882 school buildings are excluded from this phase.
Construction predated the Great Fire and site lay west of the principal burned district.
Basement, still in course of erection at the fire, first occupied in August 1872; 1873 interior work is a separate phase.
State Street bridge rendered impassable in 1871 fire
Municipal infrastructure funded partly through Illinois canal-refund appropriation.
One of eight named bridges repaired immediately and completed within one year of the fire.
State Street viaduct rendered impassable in 1871 fire
Municipal infrastructure funded partly through Illinois canal-refund appropriation.
One of three named viaducts repaired immediately and completed within one year of the fire.
Lake Superior brownstone; central glazed court
Promoted in 1872 as fireproof, with fire plugs and hose on each hall; claim is not treated as tested performance.
Nearly complete October 5 1872; three 22.5-foot facades and a central 30-foot glazed court. Chicagology rebuilding098.
Temporary City Hall and Court House
southeast corner Adams and LaSalle Streets
city offices, courts, recorder and law library
brick masonry built around former water-tank substructure
city and county offices destroyed in 1871 fire
Hastily built permanent-looking municipal replacement within the fire district; Andreas calls it a pile of brick and mortar lacking conveniences.
Authorized within a week of the fire, covered about 178 feet square, completed and occupied by January 1 1872, and cost about $75,000 furnished.
Van Buren Street crossing South Branch
Van Buren Street bridge rendered impassable in 1871 fire
Municipal infrastructure funded partly through Illinois canal-refund appropriation.
One of eight named bridges repaired immediately and completed within one year of the fire.
Wells Street bridge rendered impassable in 1871 fire
Municipal infrastructure funded partly through Illinois canal-refund appropriation.
One of eight named bridges repaired immediately and completed within one year of the fire.
Wells Street viaduct rendered impassable in 1871 fire
Municipal infrastructure funded partly through Illinois canal-refund appropriation.
One of three named viaducts repaired immediately and completed within one year of the fire.
china, glassware, guns and cutlery retail
Iron-front commercial construction; relationship to fire limits requires parcel review.
Contemporary June 1872 account says the building had been erected and opened; architect attribution is unconfirmed. Chicagology rebuilding107.
172-176 Lake Street between LaSalle and Fifth Avenue
St. Louis pressed brick with brownstone trim
Masonry mercantile construction within the rebuilt business district.
Contemporary October 1872 notice says just completed; about 60 by 144 feet with deeper basement, steam heat and elevators. Chicagology rebuilding155.
Permanent hotel rebuilding on the old site; completion belongs to 1873.
Construction began immediately after the fire and continued through 1872; opened in 1873, reported building cost about $190,000.
Church of the Messiah property sold for commercial use after the fire
Foundation stone laid fall 1872; cornerstone May 13 and dedication November 16 1873.
Recorded as a foundation phase only; cost about $90,000 and seating about 800 upon completion.
Michigan Avenue between Sixteenth and Eighteenth Streets
First Universalist Church at Van Buren and Wabash lost in 1871 fire
Stone replacement farther south; direct ordinance evidence not located.
Construction began in 1872 and completed summer 1873; incomplete spire should not be counted as later separate building.
Permanent replacement after a temporary post-fire chapel.
Rebuilding began about mid-1872 and dedication occurred May 4 1873; reported total cost including lot and organ about $100,000.
block bounded Jackson, Quincy, LaSalle and Clark Streets
W. W. Boyington; John A. Rice operational guidance
Grand Pacific Hotel I destroyed in 1871 fire
Urgent post-fire reconstruction began before plans were complete; completion belongs to 1873.
Andreas includes the $1 million project among the major first-year starts; not counted as completed in 1872.
Lake Shore and Michigan Southern / Chicago Rock Island Passenger Depot
southwest corner LaSalle and Van Buren Streets; head of LaSalle Street
Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railway; Chicago Rock Island & Pacific Railroad
Large stone public-transport reconstruction in the post-fire city.
Andreas lists the depot among first-year projects; an August 1872 contemporary notice records the third story rising. Completion belongs to 1873. Chicagology rebuilding035.
southwest corner Clark and Adams Streets
nearly completed pre-fire Lakeside Building destroyed in 1871 fire
Rebuilt with an explicit fire-resistant objective; completion belongs to 1873.
Active rebuilding documented throughout 1872 after more than $100,000 pre-fire work was lost; Chicagology rebuilding010 transcribes contemporary notices.
State Street from Monroe toward Quincy and Wabash Avenue
masonry hotel; foundations survived the fire
Palmer House I destroyed in 1871 fire
A leading attempt at fire-resistant hotel construction; contemporary 'entirely fireproof' language is recorded as aspiration, not verified performance.
Major construction continued through 1872; opening belongs to late 1873. Do not count as a 1872 completion.
northwest corner Clark and Randolph Streets
William W. Boyington; Charles W. Cregar
Sherman House II destroyed in 1871 fire
Major hotel reconstruction in the burned district; completion belongs to 1873.
Andreas lists the $650,000 Sherman House among first-year projects but its opening was May 1 1873. Chicagology rebuilding004 has a conflicting 1872 life-span label; event dating follows Andreas.
St. Michael's Church destroyed in 1871 fire
Major repair of fire-damaged church; direct code evidence not located.
Church repair was rapidly pushed at reported cost $40,000 while temporary worship continued; ready for occupancy fall 1873. Exact 1872 work fraction unknown.
Tremont House III destroyed in 1871 fire
Major stone-front hotel replacement; completion belongs to 1873.
Contractor biography says a partnership dissolved after finishing Tremont work in 1872, but hotel chronology gives 1873 completion/opening; treated as 1872 construction phase only.
Wheelock & Thomas; Julius H. Huber (1889 work)
cast-iron base; precast concrete upper facade
One of the few surviving Loop structures from the immediate post-fire rebuilding; 1889 work must be separated.
Official date range is 1872-1874. Huber's steel-framed atrium, two added stories and lower-floor redesign belong to 1889.
shore end at Chicago Water Works; lake crib; planned cross-city extension to Canal A
Municipal water infrastructure; building-code context not applicable.
Contract work commenced July 12 1872 at shore end and October 2 at crib end; completion deadline July 1 1874.
227-235 West Lake Street and 173-191 North Franklin Street
227-235 W Lake St & 173-191 N Franklin St
masonry mercantile lofts with cast-iron columns
Direct product of rebuilding after the 1871 fire; official narrative identifies characteristic post-fire commercial architecture.
Official date range is 1872-1875 and does not identify which surviving component began in 1872; retained as a start-year group record pending parcel-level permit research.
St. James church ruined in 1871 fire
Permanent reconstruction from surviving/ruined church fabric; work interrupted by 1873 financial crisis.
Rebuilding moved vigorously in 1872, stopped in 1873, resumed 1874, and first service in completed building occurred in 1875.
Institutional fire reconstruction; direct ordinance evidence not located.
Partly restored in 1872 and completed in 1876; completion must not be assigned to 1872.
Central Park at the western termination of Washington Street; later Garfield Park
West Chicago Park Commissioners and civic sponsors
salvaged burnt safes and masonry relics
A memorial reuse of fire debris, not an occupied building.
Cornerstone laid October 30 1872; project was never completed and remnants were later removed and sold as scrap. Chicagology rebuilding086 transcribes contemporary accounts.
Post-fire hotel, but no 1873 construction event is established.
Finished late in 1872 and opened February 3, 1873. Included only to prevent the architecture-summary wording from inflating the 1873 completion count.
site of the pre-fire Alexian Hospital
Alexian Brothers; Chicago Relief and Aid Society contributed $18,000
brick; two stories over large cut-stone basement; mansard roof
Alexian Brothers' Hospital destroyed in 1871 fire
Brick-and-stone institutional replacement in the burned district; no ordinance-specific evidence located.
Completed in 1873 on the old site, with capacity for more than 100 patients.
Masonry hotel construction; direct code-compliance evidence not located.
Built in 1873 by John Keller and opened October 1 by William L. Newman; 112 rooms. Address and full canonical spelling need directory confirmation because the scan heading is degraded.
red brick with stone; six stories
pre-fire Briggs House on same site
Masonry replacement begun immediately after the fire; direct code-compliance evidence not located.

Andreas says construction commenced immediately after the fire and the hotel reopened in 1873, but does not explicitly state the completion year; recorded as approximate and reviewable. Dimensions about 80 by 144 feet; reported building cost $190,000.
Brick public-school construction in the post-fire expansion period; code-specific evidence not stated.
Andreas's construction table records a 71-by-81-foot three-story brick building heated by furnaces with 758 sittings and total value $26,500.
Crosby's Opera House site; Washington Street between State and Dearborn Streets
Permanent commercial rebuilding in the burned district; no direct code-compliance statement located.
Andreas lists it among prominent 1873 completions and explicitly identifies the old Crosby Opera House site.
Chicago Gas Light and Coke Company Bridgeport Works
foot of Deering Street in Bridgeport
Chicago Gas Light and Coke Company
Industrial utility outside the principal burned core; fire-limit building-code implications were not established.
Company bought the site and erected works in 1873 to serve the southwestern city at a reported cost of $150,000; Andreas says it was connected by mains to the other works.
Chicago Public Library Book Room in the Old Water Tank
southeast corner LaSalle and Adams Streets
public library book room and reading room
City of Chicago; Chicago Public Library
Adaptive reuse of fire-surviving infrastructure, not new-code construction.
Chicago Public Library opened January 1, 1873 in the circular water tank. Recorded as a conversion/opening, not a newly erected building.
corner Washington Street and Fifth Avenue
Andreas presents it as an illustration of efforts toward fire-resistant post-fire construction; the claim is not upgraded to modern fireproof status.
Andreas and Chamberlin list it among 1873 completions; an October 1872 contemporary construction account identifies the architect and corner location.
Permanent masonry-era church following post-fire institutional relocation; code specifics not stated.
Foundation stone laid fall 1872, cornerstone May 13, 1873, dedicated November 16, 1873; auditorium seated 800 and total cost about $90,000.
northwest corner Wabash Avenue and Monroe Street
W. A. Jenkins and Ira Holmes
fine brick; six stories above basement
pre-fire Clifton House; temporary Clifton at Washington and Halsted
Brick replacement in the fire district; source gives no ordinance-specific claim.
Completed in the latter part of 1873 and opened that year; 80 feet on Wabash by about 180 feet deep, 225 rooms, building cost $237,400 and furniture $105,000.
Clybourn Place crossing of the North Branch
combination Howe truss with iron turntable
A permanent municipal transport improvement; not a building-code case.
Built in 1873; length 140 feet and cost $13,700.
Cook County farm near the County Infirmary
brick addition and added fourth story
Cook County Insane Asylum building of 1870
Institutional masonry enlargement; code-specific fire-resistance evidence not stated.

A large addition was constructed and a fourth story added to the original building in 1873, increasing capacity to about 350 patients. Recorded as a phase of the asylum complex rather than a separate institution.
First Methodist Episcopal Church Block IV
southeast corner Clark and Washington Streets
First Methodist Episcopal Church property destroyed in 1871
Post-fire mixed-use masonry replacement; commercial rents supported the congregation, while source evidence does not establish full fireproof construction.
Plans were complete by May 1872 and the 1874 directory locates the completed church block. The 1873 life-span assignment is retained with review because an exact dedication date was not located.
Fulton Street Methodist Episcopal Church Chapel
corner Fulton Street and Artesian Avenue
Outside the principal burned core; no fire-code inference.
Building began August 9, was completed in October at a cost of $4,000, and was dedicated November 2, 1873.
Grace Methodist Episcopal Church destroyed in 1871 fire
More substantial replacement after a temporary post-fire chapel; source does not establish code details.
Rebuilding began about mid-1872 and dedication occurred May 4, 1873; cost including lot and organ about $100,000; main room seated 1,500.
No post-fire code claim; this was new south-side congregational construction.
A lot was purchased and a building erected and dedicated July 27, 1873; the congregation later united into Sixth Presbyterian Church.
block bounded Jackson, Quincy, LaSalle and Clark Streets
W. W. Boyington; John A. Rice (operational guidance)
Grand Pacific Hotel I destroyed in 1871 fire
Rebuilding began with urgency before plans were complete; the replacement was larger and costlier, but the source warns that 'fireproof' remained an unsettled claim.
Completed and opened in June 1873. Andreas reports a cost near $1 million in its architecture list and describes the reconstruction as guided operationally by John A. Rice.
Neighborhood church outside the principal burned commercial core; no ordinance-level fire-code evidence found.

Scholarly history states that the first church was built in 1873. It must not be conflated with the extant monumental church begun in 1905 and completed in 1906; precise first-building parcel and demolition date need parish-archive review.
northeast corner Fifth Avenue and Washington Street
northeast corner Wells and Washington Streets
A. C. Hesing; Illinois Staats-Zeitung Company
cut limestone front; Italian Renaissance; presses in basement
Contemporary plans described substantial stone construction but do not establish comprehensive fireproofing; a later two-story fireproof addition was separate.
The newspaper reported taking full possession by April 8 1873. Dimensions were 40 feet on Washington by 110 on Fifth Avenue with about 30 offices and one elevator.
Lake Front at Michigan Avenue and Adams Street
A showpiece of post-fire recovery; its construction system and temporary-exposition character should not be generalized to ordinary code compliance.
Opened September 25, 1873. Art Institute archive metadata gives approximately 200 by 800 feet and more than 300 exhibitors; the official catalogue is contemporary evidence.
Brick municipal replacement after the fire; the building's destruction the next year shows that masonry did not eliminate fire vulnerability.
Andreas's table records a 76-by-84-foot three-story brick building with 976 sittings and value $42,000; narrative says it was occupied only one year before burning in 1874.
Brick public-school construction in the post-fire expansion period; code-specific evidence not stated.
Andreas's table records a 71-by-81-foot three-story brick building with 1,004 sittings and total value $27,000.
northwest corner LaSalle and Madison Streets
Buena Vista sandstone; plate glass; iron and zinc cresting
A contemporary 1873 account explicitly promoted it as fireproof; the database records that historical claim without asserting modern fireproof performance.

Completed for occupancy after being four stories high in October 1872. A contemporary description gives dimensions of about 53 by 81 feet and cost near $200,000; Chamberlin includes it among 1873 completions.
Lake Shore & Michigan Southern and Chicago, Rock Island & Pacific Passenger Depot
southwest corner LaSalle and Van Buren Streets
LaSalle Street at Van Buren Street
Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railway; Chicago, Rock Island & Pacific Railroad
Joliet limestone masonry depot and train shed
